Field manual

What this site is, how to use it, and where everything comes from. Plain text, no tricks.

What this is

Tech & AI Power Map is an independent research tool from AI Signals. It maps who controls artificial intelligence and Big Tech: about 140 companies, funds and governments, the money and ownership that connect them, their government contracts, their ties to the Pentagon and intelligence agencies, and the people who move between them.

It is built from the public record: company filings, government contract databases, court records, official announcements and news reporting. Every fact links to its source. Anything not confirmed is labeled unverified. A connection on this map is a fact, not an accusation.

Who it's for

  • Journalists and researchers: sourced leads, citations and the open-questions board.
  • Investors: company files, money flows, stress tests and the daily Opening Bell.
  • Anyone curious about who really runs the technology everyone uses.

Getting around

  • Bottom bar: jump to any room.
  • Top-left bar: Back, Forward, Home and Sound on/off. The trail next to it shows where you are.
  • Glowing pads: tap one to open that company or filter the page.
  • Knobs: drag up or down, or tap, to change what the page shows.
  • Drop-downs: tap any heading with a + to open it.
  • Keyboard: Alt + ← / → to go back or forward; Esc closes full-screen views.

The rooms

  • The opening command center. Live counters, the Subject Matrix (64 biggest companies, a pad flashes when there's fresh news), the Surveillance Sweep radar and the Intercepts feed. Below it: Classified, the Opening Bell and shortcuts to every room.
  • Pick any company. You get a radar of everything it's connected to, a plain-English summary, who runs it, who owns it, money in and out, government contracts, agency ties, hiring, contacts, news, and a Deep Research File (bull vs bear case, balance sheet, who controls it, supply chain, China exposure, lawsuits and open questions).
  • Every company on one board. Rows are size, columns are sector, lines are deals. Tap a sector pad to light it up; use the Links knob to show only ownership, money or deal lines.
  • Stress tests (what breaks if a company disappears), power rankings, money flows, red flags and what to watch.
  • How tech plugs into the Pentagon and spy agencies: the revolving door, defense programs, tech-defense deals and every military or intel tie.
  • The late-night read: Flock cameras and the surveillance state, drones and robots built for war, AI that went off-script, and a Defend Yourself checklist. Press Lights off.
  • Government contracts, grouped with drop-downs and sub-drop-downs, each with amount and source.
  • Ties to the CIA, NSA, Pentagon, DOGE, China's military and more, agency by agency.
  • PhD-level research papers on the forces behind the map, plus the Unknowns board: every open question nobody has answered publicly.
  • Ask anything in plain English. The AI analyst answers from this site's data and cites it.
  • The latest stories on every company, newest first.
  • Who runs what, board overlaps and who moved where.
  • Who's hiring the general public, layoffs, training programs and how to apply.
  • Lawsuits, regulators and weak spots.
  • AI spending and the policy moves in Washington and Beijing.

How often it updates

  • Every weekday before the open: the Opening Bell (futures, movers on the map, today's calendar).
  • Every Monday: company values, funding rounds, deals, news, contracts and agency ties.

Using it for a story

Every company file has a Copy citation button and a link straight to that file. Always click through to the original source before you publish; this site is a map to the record, not a substitute for it.

Fine print

  • Not investment advice. Nothing here tells you to buy or sell anything.
  • Public record only. No leaked, hacked or private data.
  • AI helps gather and organize the research. Errors are possible; sources are always shown so you can check.
  • The terminal look is a design style. This is not a government website.

For journalists & researchers

For journalists & researchers

Free to use with credit

Use this map as a starting point for research and reporting. Every fact links to where it came from, so you can check it yourself before you publish. Each company file has buttons to copy a citation and a direct link.

How to cite this site
How sure are we?
Source linkConfirmed by a filing, official release or named news report. Tap “source” to read it. ReportedIn the press but not confirmed by the companies. UnverifiedSources disagreed or we could not confirm it with a 2026 source. Treat as a lead, not a fact. CeilingThe most a contract can pay, not money spent.
MethodPublic company values are market caps at the Oct 14–15, 2026 close; private values are the latest funding round. Tiers group companies by value. A connection is a documented ownership stake, investment, or chip, cloud or supply deal, drawn from investor to company and from seller to buyer. Data was gathered Oct 15–16, 2026 and refreshes every Monday.
Download the dataSpreadsheet files (CSV) you can open in Excel or Google Sheets, with source links included.

Who’s hiring · what this screen isWhich companies are hiring, which are cutting, what jobs are open to the general public (no degree needed), where, and how to apply. Use the knobs or filters to narrow it down, then open a company for its careers link.

Hiring status, roles open to the general public, training programs and how to apply, from each company’s official careers pages and 2026 hiring news. Always apply through the official careers link.

The paper trail · government contracts

Government contracts · what this screen isMoney governments have awarded to these companies: contracts, grants, loans and subsidies. Tap a company to open its agencies, then tap an agency to see each award with amount, date and source.

Contracts, grants, loans and subsidies from governments to every company on this map. “Ceiling” is the most a contract can pay; “obligated” is money actually committed. Totals add documented figures and mix both, so read them as scale, not exact spend. Shared ceilings (JWCC, the CIA’s C2E cloud) and OneGov savings estimates are shown on each row but left out of totals so they aren’t counted twice.
